candidateRows: Rational belief requires good evidence, but both Christians and atheists may rationally reach different conclusions from the evidence.
This move defines the debate's central standard of rationality, allocates burdens of justification, and states Justin's qualified defense of Christian rationality.
At the beginning of his opening statement, Justin defines rational belief and distinguishes disagreement or falsity from necessarily being irrational.
Christian belief can be rationally grounded in personal experience, while objective investigation also supports Christianity as an intellectually compelling worldview.
The move supplies both an experiential route to warranted Christian belief and the intellectual-investigation basis for the constructive case that follows.
Justin distinguishes subjective religious experience from objective evidence and explains that sustained investigation transformed his challenged youthful belief into intellectual conviction.
Cosmic fine-tuning and the mathematical intelligibility of nature are better explained by a designing mind than by unguided luck.
This is a principal positive argument for God, using two features of the physical universe to compare theistic design with atheist-materialist coincidence.
Justin appeals to life-permitting physical constants and the effectiveness of abstract mathematics in describing nature as evidence that a mind intended an intelligible universe.
Objective human dignity, rights, and moral obligations fit Christianity's doctrine of humans made in God's image better than atheist materialism.
The argument directly contrasts the rival worldviews' capacity to ground objective value and morality, a major component of the cumulative Christian case.
Justin argues that science describes facts but cannot generate moral oughts, whereas creation in God's image and Christ's sacrifice provide a basis for equal human worth.
Deterministic atheist materialism undermines trust in reasoning, whereas God can ground genuine freedom and rationally formed beliefs.
This self-defeat argument targets the rational credentials of the opposing worldview and offers divine creation as the proposed guarantor of reason itself.
Justin contends that beliefs fixed wholly by non-rational material causes are not reached through reasoning, while God-created freedom makes rational deliberation intelligible.
The resurrection is the most reasonable explanation of widely accepted historical facts surrounding Jesus and the emergence of Christianity.
The move connects the preceding case for God specifically to Christianity by defending its central historical claim and Jesus's associated claim to divinity.
Justin lists crucifixion, the empty tomb, reported appearances, conversions, and early church growth, then argues that resurrection best explains this collection of facts.
Deep Christian disagreement on abortion and same-sex marriage indicates that alleged divine revelation is too unclear to reliably produce rational conclusions.
The move uses doctrinal and moral disagreement among recipients of the same alleged revelation to challenge its clarity, divine provenance, and rational reliability.
Justin's claim that Christianity supplies a coherent account of objective human value and morality.
After polling the Christian-majority audience, Stephen argues that sharply different moral conclusions from one supposedly divine message count against its expected clarity.
Christian accommodation of evolution reflects correction by overwhelming scientific evidence rather than foresight or clarity in Genesis.
The historical adjustment claim supports the broader charge that Christianity follows external evidence only after resistance, weakening appeals to revelation as epistemically reliable.
Justin's contention that scientific features of the universe positively point toward God and Christian theism.
Stephen contrasts historic creationist belief and persecution of dissent with modern Christian acceptance of evolution, attributing the change to compelling scientific discoveries.
Christianity is either supported by standards that also rationalize incompatible religions, rejected by healthy evidential standards, or protected by special pleading.
This trilemma directly answers the motion by arguing that consistent evidential standards cannot uniquely establish Christianity as rational without contradiction or fallacy.
Justin's claim that subjective experience and objective considerations can make Christian belief rationally warranted.
Stephen argues that lowering evidential standards validates mutually exclusive faiths, normal standards validate none, and applying unequal standards to Christianity is special pleading.
An omnipotent and loving God would communicate Christianity clearly to everyone, so widespread unbelief, disagreement, and poor transmission evidence count against that God.
This extended divine-hiddenness and communication argument attacks the compatibility of Christianity's central divine attributes with the observed quality and consequences of its evidence.
Justin's cumulative claim that Christian theism and the resurrection are supported by compelling rational and historical evidence.

Stephen contrasts what a perfectly capable and loving communicator could achieve with contested doctrines and indirect ancient testimony, concluding that the alleged evidential arrangement is irrational.
Determinism undermines the rational justification of atheistic belief because beliefs and reasoning are not freely chosen.
This begins the argument from reason, a principal basis offered for considering naturalism less rational than Christian theism.
Stephen Woodford's claim that free will is illusory and that he did not choose his atheism.
After Woodford describes choice as illusory, Brierley asks whether causally determined beliefs can nonetheless qualify as rationally justified conclusions.
Rationality consists in aligning beliefs and actions with available reasons and evidence, not in freely choosing those beliefs.
The distinction supplies Woodford's primary defense of rational inquiry against Brierley's claim that determinism defeats reason.
Justin Brierley's contention that an unchosen, determined belief cannot be rationally justified.
Woodford separates truth from rationality and argues that rational conduct depends on correspondence with one's reasons rather than metaphysical freedom.
A wholly naturalistic causal account makes thoughts products of non-rational processes and therefore undercuts confidence in reasoning itself.
This is the fullest statement of Brierley's argument from reason and directly supports his comparative case for Christian rationality.
Stephen Woodford's account of rationality as consistency between causally acquired reasons, beliefs, and actions.
Brierley argues that determined or random brain processes provide no independent warrant for truth-directed thought and invokes the argument from reason.
If human conduct is wholly determined, ultimate moral blame and praise disappear, weakening atheistic condemnations of religious wrongdoing.
The move launches the debate's major moral argument by claiming that Woodford's worldview cannot sustain his own normative criticisms.
Stephen Woodford's deterministic worldview together with his moral condemnation of religion as harmful.
Brierley links determinism to the absence of genuine responsibility and asks how Woodford can consistently describe religious behavior as morally wrong.
Morality can arise from shared aversion to suffering, biologically grounded interests, and cooperative rules without being metaphysically ultimate.
This is Woodford's substantive secular account of morality and his principal reply to the claim that atheism permits no meaningful right or wrong.
Justin Brierley's argument that determinism eliminates moral responsibility and makes condemnation of wrongdoing incoherent.
Woodford grounds moral systems in common human needs, avoidance of suffering, and social coordination while conceding that wrongness is not ultimate.
A worldview unable to say that severe cruelty is genuinely wrong conflicts with basic human moral experience and is practically unlivable.
The argument converts the abstract grounding dispute into a comparative rationality claim that Christianity better explains indispensable moral convictions.
Stephen Woodford's claim that cruelty is wrong only relative to broadly shared human preferences rather than ultimately wrong.
Using extreme cruelty as the test case, Brierley argues that secular moral consistency exacts an unacceptable and existentially unworkable cost.
Divine mercy need not suspend justice because Jesus satisfies justice while providing the means through which God extends mercy.
The response addresses an alleged internal contradiction in Christianity and identifies the atonement as the reconciliation of two divine attributes.
Stephen Woodford's argument that mercy necessarily suspends justice, making a God who is both just and merciful incoherent.
Brierley initially accepts the apparent logical tension but argues that the Christian account of Jesus joins satisfied judgment with divine mercy.
The biblical punishment of David through the death of an innocent child conflicts with the existence of an omnipotent and omnibenevolent God.
The example supplies a concrete internal-evidence challenge to Christian moral coherence and tests whether the claimed divine attributes fit scripture.
Woodford cites the account of David's child dying as punishment and asks how such treatment of an innocent can be reconciled with perfect goodness.
Difficult Old Testament narratives do not defeat rational Christianity because they are partial, culturally situated revelations interpreted through Jesus.
This is Brierley's extended method for handling morally troubling scripture while preserving Christianity's rational and ethical credibility.
Stephen Woodford's claim that the punishment and death of David's innocent child contradict an omnibenevolent God.
Brierley invokes moral grounding, interpretive uncertainty, cultural description, and the primacy of Jesus when assessing troubling Old Testament material.
Christianity is comparatively rational because it explains existence, value, reason, meaning, love, hope, and human dignity through the story of Jesus.
The closing integrates Brierley's principal arguments and directly affirms the motion-level conclusion that Christian belief is rational and existentially explanatory.
Brierley closes by combining explanatory arguments with Christianity's account of meaning, sacrificial love, resurrection hope, and Western human dignity.
Atheism merely denotes lack of belief in God and should not be conflated with materialism or positions on free will.
The distinction directly challenges Brierley's repeated treatment of atheism and materialism as a single worldview with shared consequences.
Brierley's earlier characterization of an atheistic materialistic worldview and its consequences for love, hope, and reason.
Following Brierley's closing appeal to Christianity as the basis of Western values and hope, Woodford begins his closing statement by correcting the scope of atheism.
Christian supernatural claims require evidence proportionate to their extraordinary character, which transmitted testimony and apparent wonders do not supply.
The move states and illustrates the principal evidential standard by which Woodford argues that Christianity's central supernatural claims are irrational to accept.
Brierley's case that testimony, historical considerations, and apparent signs provide a rational basis for Christian supernatural claims.
Woodford defines rationality in evidential terms and develops successive hypotheticals involving divine identity, apparent powers, later testimony, textual alteration, and failed cosmological claims.
Even granting the virgin birth and resurrection would not logically entail that Jesus is God's son, revealing a faith-specific double epistemology.
It attacks the inference from Christianity's headline miracle claims to Jesus's divine status and alleges that believers relax ordinary logical standards within faith.
The Christian inference that Jesus's reported virgin birth and resurrection establish his divine identity and warrant accepting Christian claims.
After the evidential hypotheticals, Woodford formalizes the Christian inference, then argues that its conclusion does not follow even if both supernatural premises are provisionally granted.
A permissive definition can label Christianity rational only by doing the same for rival religions; adequate reasons are required even for a true belief.
The conclusion directly resolves the motion by distinguishing the possible intelligence of Christians from the alleged irrationality of Christianity as a belief system.
Brierley's defense that Christianity is rational because its worldview is coherent, explanatory, practically fruitful, and supported by evidence.
Woodford qualifies that some definitions can make Christianity rational, argues those definitions indiscriminately validate other faiths, restates his account of justification, and closes.
Christianity's historical spread undercuts the claim that scripture was an obviously failed communication method, and humans cannot presume to know God's optimal purposes.
The response directly defends the rational availability of Christianity against Woodford's claim that an all-powerful God chose an inadequate and unreliable means of revelation.
Woodford's argument that an all-powerful God would not rely on an error-prone, historically transmitted book to communicate essential supernatural truth.

In the first part of his resurrection-and-scripture answer, Brierley appeals to Christianity's broad historical impact and challenges Woodford's assumed vantage point for judging divine communication.
Textual criticism, early documents, eyewitness indications, and Paul's early traditions provide substantially reliable access to first-century Christian claims.
This move supplies Brierley's main historical rebuttal to the allegation that resurrection belief rests on late, corrupted, or irrecoverable chains of testimony.
Woodford's portrayal of gospel testimony as copied, amended, contradictory transmission that cannot rationally establish Jesus or the resurrection.
Brierley moves from divine purposes to historical reliability, invoking textual criticism, scholarly consensus on Jesus's existence, early documentary proximity, and Pauline material.
Objective moral disagreement does not negate moral facts, and their justification ultimately requires a transcendent moral reality beyond the physical world.
The move defends the moral argument's key premise while conceding uncertainty on particular applications and distinguishing moral grounding from simplistic biblical rule extraction.
The audience objection that conflicting moral intuitions about animals either refute Christianity or undermine Brierley's intuition-based moral objectivity.
After addressing the cited treatment of animals, Brierley concedes uncertainty about veganism, explains his interpretive approach to scripture, and grounds evident moral facts transcendentally.
Although a fine-tuning tolerance cannot be mapped straightforwardly onto ordinary probability, its extreme precision still calls for explanation.
The concession refines rather than abandons Brierley's fine-tuning case, preserving the claimed explanatory significance while accepting a technical criticism of probabilistic framing.
The audience challenge that Brierley's fine-tuning statistic uses the wrong probability and should instead be formulated conditionally given life's existence.
Following clarification of conditional probability, Brierley distinguishes a physical tolerance range from an exact probability, acknowledges a weakness in a prior analogy, and maintains the anomaly.
Christianity can be rational for people presented with its evidential case even though many people historically lacked access to that evidence.
The answer squarely addresses whether unequal historical access defeats Christianity's rationality and distinguishes availability of evidence from the intrinsic rational force of the case.
The audience objection that Christianity is a religion of historical and cultural privilege, making it less rational than agnosticism or generic theism.

Brierley limits his rationality claim to those who encounter the Christian case, separates divine justice toward the uninformed from evidential rationality, and reaffirms Christianity as the best option.
If beliefs and reasoning are wholly reducible to nonpurposive brain chemistry, that account undercuts confidence in reason itself and requires its own faith commitment.
This reformulation removes dependence on disputed libertarian choice and preserves Brierley's central claim that a purely physical worldview cannot adequately ground rational inference.
The objection that people do not choose what evidence convinces them, weakening Brierley's attempt to connect rational belief with freely chosen alternatives.

After partially defending freedom among alternatives, Brierley pivots to a reductive account of cognition and argues that mechanical brain processes cannot themselves explain normatively rational thought.
Evolution can favor survival-enhancing irrational beliefs, so human cognition need not have evolved primarily for rationality or truth.
The move directly addresses whether naturalistic evolution can explain cognition despite selecting for survival rather than consistently rational or true beliefs.
The audience challenge that evolution toward survival does not establish reliable truth-directed belief faculties.
After an audience member raises Plantinga's evolutionary argument, Stephen uses a predator-detection example to argue that adaptive caution can preserve systematically irrational cognition.
If evolution selects cognition for survival rather than truth, then naturalism undermines confidence in the beliefs produced by evolved cognition.
This is the central self-defeat objection: Stephen's evolutionary explanation is presented as conceding that naturalism cannot warrant trust in human reasoning.
Stephen's claim that evolution can select survival-promoting irrationality rather than generally truth-directed cognition.
Justin answers Stephen's predator example by arguing that its distinction between survival and truth supports Plantinga's contention that naturalism defeats trust in evolved beliefs.
Uncertainty about evolved cognition is unavoidable but manageable through verification, and it does not justify adopting a more appealing theistic worldview.
The move supplies Stephen's principal answer to the evolutionary defeater by distinguishing fallible inquiry from an unwarranted appeal to theism.
Justin's contention that evolution for survival undercuts naturalism by defeating confidence in evolved human beliefs.
Stephen accepts that certainty is unavailable, argues that humans must use and test their evolved cognitive apparatus, and rejects theism as an escape from shared epistemic limits.
Naturalism faces a deeper problem for reason than theism because a theistic worldview can coherently ground reliance on reason and truth-directed belief.
The closing exchange directly compares the rational coherence of the two worldviews and claims that theism can ground reason where naturalism cannot.
Stephen's assertion that limited certainty is harmless for naturalism but creates a distinctive problem for Justin's worldview.
Justin rejects Stephen's asymmetry, arguing that naturalism undermines reason itself while theism makes reliance on reason and development of true beliefs coherent.
